The goal is to approach human spaceflight with the intent of ensuring that humanity will not only survive in space, but flourish.

items.title: A Dark Energy Camera Portrait of the Betta Fish Nebula
items.blurb: The Betta Fish Nebula is a supernova remnant almost 7,000 light years away. It consists of the cast off layers of a star that exploded as a supernova. When those layers slammed into the interstellar medium, the energy of the shock lit them up. The DECam has captured the best image of the Betta Fish Nebula so far.

items.blurb: Science instruments for NASA’s Dragonfly are starting to arrive at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland, where the car-sized rotorcraft is coming together for its mission to explore Saturn’s largest moon, Titan. First to check in: DragonCam, which consists of seven cameras designed to characterize Titan’s surface at multiple scales during

items.title: Why Mega-Constellations Have a Hidden Space Junk Blind Spot
items.blurb: We are consistently launching more and more stuff into space. As of now, space agencies track more than 30,000 objects larger than a softball, with an expected one million more bullet-sized pieces of debris orbiting Earth that are too small to spot from the ground.. Government agencies and private commercial entities are planning to have up to 100,000 active spacecraft in orbit by the early 2030s, turning some orbital shells into crowded highways. And according to a new paper, available in preprint on arXiv by Federico Toson, a researcher at the University of Padova in Italy, the math that regulatory agencies use to determine whether a satellite is “safe” in these highly congested spaces is fundamentally flawed.

items.title: UK-Built X-Ray Telescope Ready For Action at Mercury
items.blurb: The joint ESA/JAXA BepiColombo mission has arrived at Mercury, and among its arsenal of detectors ready to explore the innermost world is an innovative new instrument. A University of Leicester team recently released an image of an iconic deep-sky object as a proof of concept test for their Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS). This comes as BepiColombo entered orbit around Mercury this past week.

items.title: Space Lasers Are Fast, But Clouds Still Rule the Forecast
items.blurb: Since the launch of Sputnik, humanity has talked to its spacecraft through radio waves. Radio is great for communication through any weather, but it has hit a limit – traditional radio frequencies are highly regulated by bodies like the International Telecommunications Union, which limits the scalability of radio communications networks to meet the growing demand of bandwidth to and from space. The obvious solution is to switch to infrared lasers, which have an extremely high data transfer rate. However, according to a paper available in pre-print on arXiv from Dr. Slava Turyshev – best known to UT readers for his work on turning the Sun’s gravity into a giant telescope – the raw speed of laser communication isn’t the bottleneck, it’s the system’s reliability.

items.title: Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past
items.blurb: Scientists studying ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side have uncovered surprising evidence that challenges decades of thinking about the Solar System’s violent past. Instead of a single catastrophic bombardment, asteroid impacts appear to have declined gradually over billions of years, revealing new clues about Earth's early evolution and the origins of life.

items.title: A Star’s ‘Obliquity’ Likely Has Little Impact On A Given Planet’s Habitability
items.blurb: For decades, astronomers have puzzled over whether a star’s given obliquity, or axial tilt, changes over time and space. A new paper says large obliquity changes appear to be uncommon.

items.blurb: A volcanic eruption just off the southeast shore of the Pacific island has reshaped the coast, but it’s unclear how long the new land will survive.

items.title: Panic buying? Gradual stockpiling makes for better 'prepping' without emptying supermarket shelves
items.blurb: Soon after the government launched its "Be Ready" campaign, supermarket shelves were empty where the bottled water usually sits. Flashlights quickly went out of stock too.

items.title: Copper aluminum oxide could make light-controlling components for smart glasses 120 times thinner
items.blurb: Could augmented reality (AR) glasses become as thin and lightweight as everyday eyeglasses? Researchers at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) and their collaborators have identified a material that could reduce the thickness of polarization-control components to approximately 1/120 that of conventional components while maintaining high light transmission. The discovery could pave the way for smaller, lighter AR devices and more compact optical communication equipment.

items.title: What is resilience? It may be less about bouncing back than we think
items.blurb: Resilience can sound empowering. Yet it can also become a responsibility, a socially imposed burden that people are expected to demonstrate when they are ill, aging or struggling.

items.title: DebunkBot can quash emerging conspiracy theories
items.blurb: Rumors immediately began circulating after Donald Trump, then a presidential candidate, survived an assassination attempt during an open-air rally on July 13, 2024. Some suspected the "deep state" was responsible, while others thought it was a false flag operation to get Trump reelected.

items.title: Highly sociable Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins with predictable group size preferences may live longer
items.blurb: Aging can bring changes in sociability, such as decreased network size, increased social selectivity, reduced social influence and connectedness and reduced affiliative interactions. A study published Nov. 24 in the open-access journal PLOS Biology by Kelley Caroline Meehan at The University of Queensland, St. Lucia, Australia, and colleagues suggests a relationship in Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins between sociability (group size), its predictability and longevity.

items.title: Scientists pinpoint DNA copying 'traffic jams' impacting genome stability
items.blurb: Creating an accurate copy of the genome—the entire length of DNA in a cell—is the fundamental step before cells can divide, the basis on which all life sits. Errors in that duplication process—including replication pauses—lead to natural genetic changes that underpin evolution, but also give rise to diseases such as cancer.

items.title: No Pumbaa Needed: Meerkats Are Great Solo Navigators
items.blurb: But they’re still best off sticking with their gangs

items.title: Effort can deepen understanding without making learning more enjoyable, study suggests
items.blurb: As children, many of us resisted being told that studying harder would make learning enjoyable, especially when struggling with math homework. Yet as adults, we may give children the same advice. But does effort really lead to interest, or is it the other way around?

items.title: Iron nanoparticles help light-based therapy destroy missed cancer cells
items.blurb: Some cancer cells slip past even the most precise treatments and then grow back. Researchers at Nagoya University in Japan may have found a way to reach them. The team improved a light-based cancer treatment by adding tiny iron particles. In mice, their therapy shrank tumors more effectively and killed nearby cancer cells that the original treatment cannot target. Called a "photothermal bystander effect," this offers a new way of reaching cancer cells that would otherwise survive. The treatment also grew stronger with each round of light.

items.title: Selective logging can better preserve subtropical forest adaptive capacity than clear-cutting
items.blurb: Adaptive capacity—the ability to cope with disturbances and environmental change—offers a useful perspective for sustainable forest management. However, applying this concept to logging remains challenging, and a key question is how different logging practices affect forest adaptive capacity.

items.title: Biologists sort bacteria-killing peptides by speed: Slow is smooth, smooth is more effective
items.blurb: A quick kill is not always best when battling bacterial infections. Sometimes, as new Stanford research shows, slower is better.

items.title: Birds respond more quickly to predators in habitats with greater species diversity
items.blurb: The diversity of species in a habitat is a common focus of conservation efforts. Local biodiversity has been shown to influence important ecosystem functions like pollination and pest control. In this study, Kumar and colleagues investigated the impact of diversity on the flow of ecological information in the form of defensive bird calls.

items.title: New system enables highly sensitive detection of trace hydrogen
items.blurb: A research team led by professor Fang Yonghua at the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science of the Chinese Academy of Sciences has developed a new system for detecting trace amounts of hydrogen that improves detection sensitivity by reducing background interference, enabling it to directly detect hydrogen at a concentration of one part per million (ppm).

items.title: A unified framework for carbon dioxide removal—with an ocean view
items.blurb: When it comes to reducing atmospheric carbon, most roads lead to the sea. That's only natural, since the ocean is Earth's largest accessible repository for CO₂. Even without interventions to enhance its ability to capture carbon, the ocean holds about 50 times more carbon than the atmosphere and more than 20 times more carbon than plants, animals and soil combined.

items.title: Getting blood out of bone
items.blurb: "Jurassic Park" gave us a mosquito in amber, dinosaur DNA and a fantastic argument against opening a theme park. No mosquitoes were needed for this recent discovery, because the dinosaur fossil preserved its own bloody evidence of a land before time.

items.title: New theoretical model allows for sustained entanglement between diamond qubits at greater separations
items.blurb: In a new study accepted in the journal Physical Review B, a team of physicists from the University of Delaware may have found a way to overcome limitations in maintaining the entanglement of diamond qubits. The model involves driving the qubits away from equilibrium using microwave radiation while the surrounding material is allowed to remain in equilibrium. The approach allows for both long-range and steady-state entanglement of the qubits. The paper is published on the arXiv preprint server.

items.title: Simple 'grow-and-repel' rule explains how brain immune cells organize themselves to protect nervous tissue
items.blurb: Imagine you need to cover a large territory with trees, ensuring no gaps are left. What is the most efficient way to plant them? This is the spatial puzzle faced by microglia, the immune cells of our brain. During development, these cells must spread across the nervous tissue to monitor and protect, yet there is no central coordinator: each cell senses only its immediate surroundings.

items.title: New research reveals a bias in employee reference checks
items.blurb: When managers are asked to provide a reference for an employee, they may be doing more than describing that person's performance. They may also be promoting themselves.

items.title: Four decades of citizen science reveal widespread declines in native plant distributions in Japan
items.blurb: A new study led by researchers at Kyushu University has found that nearly 45% of 1,864 native plant species surveyed across Kanagawa Prefecture, Japan, were recorded in fewer locations over approximately four decades. The findings, published in Communications Biology on Sept. 15, 2026, show how long-running citizen science surveys can reveal biodiversity changes that conventional assessments focused on threatened species may miss.

items.title: Tiny tracker reveals the longest ever recorded hummingbird migration
items.blurb: Small though they may be, hummingbirds are no slouches when it comes to long-distance flight. These tiny birds can migrate thousands of miles across countries and continents. And now researchers have revealed the longest hummingbird migration to date—an impressive 6,526-kilometer journey (4,055 miles) from Alabama to Alaska in just 38 days.

items.title: Does Junk Food Alter Brain Function More in Younger People?
items.blurb: Scientists gave them milkshakes to find out

items.title: Ice near Antarctica's surface could unlock climate clues millions of years old
items.blurb: Some of the oldest clues to Earth's climate history lie surprisingly close to Antarctica's surface. Researchers at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB) are exploring the potential of these ancient archives, with a new scientific perspective coinciding with two Antarctic field expeditions.

items.title: Water signals could guide future efforts to image supermassive black hole shadows
items.blurb: University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa researchers are exploring a new way to study some of the universe's most mysterious objects: supermassive black holes.

items.title: Having fun learning with an app like Duolingo? You might be learning less than you think
items.blurb: Apps like Duolingo aim to make learning as enjoyable as possible. But enjoyment can also make you feel you are learning more than you actually are. This is the finding of research by Tilburg marketing researchers Robert Smith and Anna Paley. In an experiment with a language-learning app, participants who completed a more enjoyable learning task believed that they learned more than they actually did. The study is published in the Journal of Marketing Research.

items.title: Deep-sea clam discovered living inside the throat of a sea urchin
items.blurb: A new species of bivalve has been discovered living inside the esophagus of a deep-sea urchin in one of the most unusual partnerships known among clams. Named Vaticinaria gulicola, it was found on the abyssal seafloor of the Great Australian Bight, at depths of about 4,000 to 5,000 meters (13,100 to 16,400 feet).

items.title: Two AI companies reveal ‘Earth-shattering’ solutions to major maths problem
items.blurb: Anthropic and OpenAI reported proofs of the same maths problem on the same day – a step that could help solve the monumental conundrum known as P versus NP

items.title: Designing and optimizing genetic circuits in biology
items.blurb: Although genetic circuits are important tools in synthetic biology and related fields, such as health care and sustainable manufacturing, designing them to function reliably can be challenging and often requires extensive laboratory testing and optimization.

items.title: Four radiation belts surrounded Earth for weeks after 2024 solar superstorm
items.blurb: Within Earth's magnetic field, energetic particles are trapped in two doughnut-shaped regions known as the Van Allen radiation belts—usually separated by a gap where particles are especially sparse. This structure can be dramatically rearranged during solar storms, but until now, astronomers have remained largely unsure as to how this happens.

items.title: The mystery of sub-Neptunes – the planets we thought shouldn’t exist
items.blurb: Sub-Neptunes are the most abundant exoplanets, but are unlike anything in our solar system. We are finally gaining tantalising clues about what they are and how they came to be

items.title: Offshore wind turbine hum may make phytoplankton grow faster
items.blurb: They are single-celled, tiny and vital to life on Earth. Phytoplankton, which drift freely in the water column, provide food and oxygen for other marine organisms, while consuming CO₂ and nutrients—much like plants on land.

items.title: Guinea baboons respond flexibly to changing environmental conditions
items.blurb: Climate change is affecting the environmental conditions of wildlife around the world: Rising temperatures, changing precipitation patterns and more frequent extreme weather events can lead to important food sources becoming unavailable, at least temporarily. How well animals cope with such changes also depends on how flexibly they can adapt their behavior to new conditions.

items.title: Ancient cellular machinery boosts immunity against cancer
items.blurb: Cornell researchers have found a novel way to boost immunity against cancer: using ancient virus-derived machinery to produce tiny extracellular vesicles that carry antigen information across long distances to rally immune cells.

items.title: Q&A: How socioeconomic status is measured can obscure inequalities in health care
items.blurb: Socioeconomic differences in health may be greater than research suggests. In a new thesis, Balram Rai used PSA testing in the Stockholm region as an example and investigated how socioeconomic position can be measured at different levels and how measurement errors can affect inferences about inequalities in health.

items.title: Roads store microplastics before they join rain runoff to waterways
items.blurb: QUT researchers have developed a modeling framework to quantify microplastic inputs from urban surfaces to ecologically sensitive water environments such as Moreton Bay.

items.title: The Flower with a Flame Inside
items.blurb: Behold the skunk cabbage. It produces the highest rate of energy of any organism on Earth. Also, it switches sexes.

items.title: Will AI Permanently Change Our Idea of Beauty?
items.blurb: AI models generate more attractive faces than real human ones—setting a new unattainable beauty standard for all of us

items.title: 18 brilliant and surprising gifts for science lovers this Christmas
items.blurb: No more periodic table socks! New Scientist’s staff are full of inspiration for eclectic and unexpected presents for science lovers this festive season

items.title: Severe eczema healed by novel immune-calming pill in clinical trial
items.blurb: An experimental drug has been found to be highly effective and safe for treating moderate to severe eczema in a clinical trial and has the advantage of being taken in pill form rather than injected

items.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick
items.blurb: A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck has revealed sophisticated waterproofing techniques involving pine tar and beeswax. Microscopic pollen grains trapped in the ancient coatings are now helping scientists reconstruct where the vessel may have traveled and undergone repairs more than two millennia ago.

items.title: Toddlers form complex memories but may then lose access to them
items.blurb: Few of us can remember events from our earliest years, but that might be because we lose the ability to recall memories - not because we didn't make them in the first place

items.title: Is mental illness universal?
items.blurb: Do all cultures experience the same mental disorders? Or are our experiences of mental distress culturally specific? - by Alexander Pereira Read on Aeon

items.title: Cannabis users develop psychosis years earlier, and the gap grows with age
items.blurb: A major analysis of 149 studies found that cannabis users develop psychosis an average of 2.5 years earlier than non-users, with the difference growing to more than six years among adults 30 and older. Researchers warn that cannabis-related psychiatric risks may accumulate over time, challenging the belief that using marijuana after adolescence is relatively safe.

items.title: Scientists discover a new type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat
items.blurb: Researchers have discovered a new subtype of depression that may affect nearly one in four people with severe, recurrent, or persistent depression. Known as "circadian depression," it is linked to the body's internal clock and is associated with night owl tendencies, excessive sleep, persistent exhaustion, and more severe symptoms. Traditional antidepressants often work less effectively for these individuals, potentially explaining why some people struggle to find relief.

items.title: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it
items.blurb: Scientists have uncovered surprising evidence that Earth’s next ice age may have already begun, only to be stopped by global warming. By studying ancient plants preserved beneath the Barnes Ice Cap in the Canadian Arctic, researchers discovered that the remnants of a massive ice sheet began expanding again about 2,000 years ago, signaling the possible start of a new glacial period. But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.

items.title: Super El Niño is making the global omega-3 shortage much worse
items.blurb: There is already a scarcity of the long-chain omega-3s that are critical to our health, and this year’s massive El Niño is making it much worse. Columnist Michael Le Page says we have a solution – we just need to use it

items.title: The technology that could make government internet blackouts impossible
items.blurb: Direct-to-cell technology could one day provide a lifeline for getting around authoritarian regimes’ internet shutdowns, but international law and technical limitations are holding the technology back for now

items.title: Funding must work better for SMEs to tackle energy challenges, finds research
items.blurb: Scotland's small food and drink businesses face significant financial and operational barriers that could see them frozen out of vital funding to cut emissions from keeping produce cold, according to research from Heriot-Watt University.

items.title: Workplace absenteeism: Why temporary disability is a right, not an expense
items.blurb: Temporary disability is a cornerstone of the public Social Security system. It is a right for all workers who fall ill and a social security benefit designed primarily to protect those who are sick, enabling them to receive medical treatment and recover or improve their condition while ensuring they have sufficient income during periods in which they are unable to work.

items.title: New light-conversion tool could help speed up quantum computing
items.blurb: Want to break down some basics in the world of quantum research over dinner? Researchers at the Cockrell School of Engineering have you covered.

items.title: AI has solved a host of big math problems—here's why this threatens the whole field of mathematics
items.blurb: For many, the year 2026 will be remembered as the one when mathematics had an identity crisis and forever changed. Frontier (cutting-edge) AI models made by OpenAI and Anthropic made stunning progress on hundreds of open problems that have baffled mathematicians for decades—and centuries in some cases.

items.title: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history
items.blurb: Earth’s journey from an oxygen-starved world to a planet capable of supporting complex life may have unfolded very differently than scientists once believed. A new analysis suggests that oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere in three major stages, with the oceans taking millions or even hundreds of millions of years to catch up.

items.title: Do a violin's physical characteristics really improve with regular playing?
items.blurb: There is a widespread notion among violinists: A violin "opens up" as it is played, which is to say its sound gradually improves. However, an experiment conducted by a team led by a CNRS researcher has challenged this belief in a study published in Acta Acustica. After six months, the professional soloist in charge of playing the violin judged the process complete, reporting that the instrument had become easier to play and its tone had improved. Yet, no physical or acoustic measurement confirmed that this feeling resulted from such a mechanical change in the instrument itself.

items.title: Genetic mosaic helps explain diverse forms of Darwin's finches
items.blurb: Darwin's finches are known for their varied beaks, which help them take advantage of different food sources in the Galápagos Islands. Much previous research has focused on seed-eating ground finches, but their relatives that search for insects in forested areas have received less attention.

items.title: Depression may be an early warning sign of Alzheimer's disease
items.blurb: Depression in older adults may be more than a mental health concern. Scientists discovered that accumulating tau protein, a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, was linked to worsening depressive symptoms in people who still had normal memory and thinking abilities. The faster tau built up in the brain, the faster depressive symptoms increased, suggesting that mood changes could emerge before cognitive decline.

items.title: Recipe for one of the world's most important cancer drugs uncovered: Tobacco plants could produce the medicine
items.blurb: More people around the world will receive a cancer diagnosis at some point in their lives. As this trend is expected to continue, researchers have been working to crack the code of how the widely used cancer drug Taxol (paclitaxel) is naturally produced, with the aim of making its production cheaper and more efficient in the future.

items.title: Local measurements reveal global quantum properties in a constant number of experimental runs
items.blurb: A quantum device with more qubits is harder to verify. Describing a general quantum state takes an exponential number of parameters, and reconstructing it in full—a procedure known as state tomography—becomes impractical as the system grows. Yet most experiments do not need the full description. They need to know a few things: Is the state close to the target? Are the qubits entangled? And does the system carry the resources needed for quantum computation?
