items.title: Syria Polio Outbreak Response | Situation Report No. 1, 22 November 2026
items.blurb:
Countries: Syrian Arab Republic, Iraq
Sources: Government of the Syrian Arab Republic, UN Children's Fund, World Health Organization

Please refer to the attached file.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

In October 2026, after receiving initial reports of children with acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) in Deir ez-Zor Governorate, Syria, the Ministry of Health (MoH) mounted a swift response, in coordination with partners.

Conflict, displacement, interrupted immunization and population movement have created immunity gaps. An unrelated variant VDPV1 detection was reported in wastewater in the area in February 2026.

HIGHLIGHTS

The MoH, supported by WHO,UNICEF and partners, is leading the outbreak response, including intensified surveillance and vaccination.

Emergency vaccination activities reached:

  • 34 720 children in October 2026
  • 54 382 in November 2026 (111% of the target of 49 000)

The high coverage can be attributed to population movement. Additional efforts are needed to determine target population in future rounds.

The next campaign is planned for 30 November 2026 in six districts of Deir ez-Zor Governorate, integrating child nutrition assessments, drinking-water chlorine level checks and chlorine distribution.

An expanded scope will follow in December 2026.

The risk of further spread within Syria and to neighbouring countries, including Iraq, remains a concern due to uneven vaccination coverage and immunity gaps, particularly among displaced, mobile and underserved populations.

COORDINATION OF THE RESPONSE

The MoH is coordinating national and subnational actors. WHO and UNICEF are mobilizing regional and global technical expertise, while the Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI) provides technical and financial support. World Vision and the International Rescue Committee funded the first two vaccination rounds in October and November 2026.

Two coordination meetings involving national, regional and global response teams have reviewed the situation and agreed on priorities. The MoH Incident Management Team meets weekly through its Emergency Operations Centre. The remaining 13 governorates in Syria have been advised to intensify surveillance and preparedness. Cross-border coordination is particularly important for Iraq, given population movements and the history of wild poliovirus transmission across this border in 2013.

items.title: Malawi – District Profile: Chikwawa (October 2026)
items.blurb:
Country: Malawi
Source: International Organization for Migration

Please refer to the attached file.

Under the Regional Response to Climate Displacement in Sub-Saharan Africa (RE2CLID) program, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) is implementing activities across eight districts in Malawi: Blantyre, Blantyre City, Chikwawa, Dowa, Mangochi, Mulanje, Nsanje and Phalombe. The district profiles bring together available data on population, climate hazards, displacement, vulnerability and local capacities in Chikwawa and will be complemented by the forthcoming RE2CLID Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) baseline assessment.

This profile is focused on Chikwawa District, which has experienced recurrent climate-related displacement associated with floods, tropical storms, cyclones and drought. The five Traditional Authorities (TAs) targeted by RE2CLID – Ngabu, Lundu, Makhwira, Maseya and Ngowe – were home to 348,079 people according to the 2018 Census, representing approximately 62 per cent of the district's population.

Historical DTM assessments show that these TAs also accounted for a high proportion of displacement recorded during major flood and storm events: approximately 94 per cent during the 2015 floods, 99 per cent during Cyclone Idai and 89 per cent following Cyclone Freddy. Patterns nevertheless varied between events. Displacement was concentrated particularly in TA Lundu during the 2015 floods and Cyclone Idai, while following Cyclone Freddy, DTM recorded 111,864 IDPs across 43 sites, with the largest shares located in TA Ngabu and TA Makhwira.

Looking ahead, the 2026/27 outlook points to a multi-hazard context. Under the DCCMS Strong El Niño scenario, Chikwawa is classified as extreme drought risk, while extreme-rainfall risk increases from no threat during October–December 2026 to extreme during January–March 2027. Understanding how historical displacement patterns intersect with current and projected climate risks can help inform anticipatory action, preparedness and targeted displacement monitoring.

items.title: World: Europe — Mixed Migration Flows to Europe, Quarterly Overview (July – September 2026)
items.blurb:
Countries: World, Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Greece, Italy, Malta, Spain, Sudan
Source: International Organization for Migration

Please refer to the attached file.

In late 2015, IOM launched a Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) Flow Monitoring system, aiming to monitor Mixed Migration Flows to Europe by land and sea. Since then, DTM gathers, validates and disseminates information on migrants and refugees entering Europe through four main routes:

  • Eastern Mediterranean route (EMR): arrivals by sea and land to Bulgaria, Cyprus and Greece
  • Central Mediterranean route (CMR): arrivals by sea to Italy and Malta
  • Western Mediterranean route (WMR): arrivals by sea to the Peninsular Coasts of Spain, Balearic Islands, by land to the autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla
  • Western African Atlantic route (WAAR): arrivals by sea to the Canary Islands of Spain

DTM also monitors data on migrants in transit through the Western Balkan route (WBR), including data from Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia, and Kosovo (UNSCR 1244, 1999). These are considered separately to prevent, to the extent possible, the double counting of the same people, crossing multiple borders. Finally, DTM compiles data on migrants entering Croatia, Romania and Slovenia by land, typically after having crossed the Western Balkans or Bulgaria.

This report presents the latest available data and trends, focusing on the third quarter of 2026 and comparing it with the same period in 2025.

  • In the third quarter of 2026 (Q3 2026), 36,097 migrants arrived in Europe via these four routes. This represents a 42 per cent increase from previous Q2 2026 and a 24 per cent decline compared with Q3 2025. The steepest year-on-year drop was on the CMR (down 59%), followed by the EMR (down 13%). Arrivals were distributed across the CMR to Italy and Malta (24%), the EMR to Greece, Cyprus and Bulgaria (42%), the WMR to Spain (25%), and the WAAR to Spain (9%).
  • According to Eurostat, EU+ countries registered over 99,385 new asylum applications in the third quarter of 2026. Although data on asylum applications remain incomplete at the time of writing, France, Italy and Greece are among the highest ranking countries in the EU27+ in Q3 of 2026. Notably, France registered nearly twice as many first-time asylum applications (27,910) than Italy (15,450) did. Between July and September 2026, the main applicants held nationalities from Afghanistan (10%), Bangladesh (7%) and Sudan (6%), comprising nearly a quarter of all applications registered. These groups are followed by Türkiye, and Pakistan, Ukraine, Syrian Arab Republic and Somalia, averaging at around 4 per cent, respectively.
  • According to IOM’s MMP, 920 migrants died or went missing at sea while trying to reach Europe through the Mediterranean and Western African Atlantic routes in Q3 of 2026. Of these, 141 perished on the Central Mediterranean, and 350 while trying to cross the Atlantic to reach the Canary Islands. This represents a 6 per cent increase compared to Q3 2025 (871).

The International Organization for Migration (IOM), in collaboration with the National Disaster Management Organization (NADMO), conducted a Post-Distribution Monitoring (PDM) exercise among households that received humanitarian assistance following the 29 June 2026 floods. A total of 134 beneficiary households were monitored to assess the effectiveness, relevance, and utilization of the support provided, as well as the extent to which it addressed the immediate needs of affected households.

The Post-Distribution Monitoring gathered feedback directly from beneficiaries on their level of satisfaction with the assistance received, challenges encountered during or after the distribution process, and the overall contribution of the assistance in supporting their recovery. It also assessed the accessibility, timeliness, and appropriateness of the assistance while identifying any remaining priority needs and gaps among flood-affected households. The findings provide valuable evidence to inform future humanitarian interventions, strengthen accountability to affected populations, and improve the quality and effectiveness of disaster response efforts.

items.title: Occupied Palestinian Territory Emergency Response Activity Update #61, 1 - 31 October 2026 [EN/AR]
items.blurb:
Country: occupied Palestinian territory
Source: International Organization for Migration

Please refer to the attached files.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

October marked both one year since the October 2025 ceasefire and three years since the escalation of hostilities. The humanitarian situation in Gaza remains dire and extremely fragile, with humanitarian partners warning that funding shortfalls, combined with ongoing Israeli restrictions, have begun to reverse the gains achieved since the ceasefire was announced. One year on, Israeli military operations have continued and approximately 70 per cent of Gaza remains behind the constantly shifting “Yellow Line”. Most of the population remains displaced in worn-out tents, overcrowded sites and severely damaged buildings, with water and sanitation systems devastated. With the rainy season imminent, conditions are likely to worsen.

Needs ahead of winter are acute. The Shelter Cluster estimates that 1.98 million people require shelter and non-food item assistance, yet the supplies available can reach fewer than one in five of those needing shelter for winter. Winter shelter requirements remained severely underfunded, with two-thirds of the USD 283 million required still unmet. Structural safety is a growing concern, with OCHA preliminary estimates – supported by IOMled assessments – indicating that more than 4,000 buildings require full or partial demolition and some 44,000 people living in over 2,300 structurally unsafe buildings.

Briefing the Security Council on 15 October, the UN Acting Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, Ramiz Alakbarov, reported that, for the fourth consecutive winter, Israeli restrictions on the entry of essential equipment, spare parts, engine oil and other supplies continued to impede humanitarian and recovery efforts, and that partners knew what winter preparedness required but lacked the materials to act at the scale required. Without expanded access, the lifting of Israeli restrictions on critical materials, and adequate funding, humanitarian actors will remain unable to move from emergency relief to the recovery that Gaza urgently needs.

items.title: The Royal Court’s new mission? To boldly go back to the 60s space race with The Afronauts
items.blurb:
Royal Court theatre, London
Ryan Calais Cameron’s ‘true(ish)’ account of a charismatic freedom fighter’s plan to take a Zambian crew to the moon never quite lifts off

Ryan Calais Cameron has proved himself a playwright of stratospheric talent. His previous plays For Black Boys Who Have Considered Suicide When the Hue Gets Too Heavy and Retrograde both streaked their way into the West End. This new one is filled with mighty ambition but does not lift off in the same way.

It is based on what he calls a “true(ish)” story. The figure of Edward Mukuka Nkoloso (Lucian Msamati) is taken from Zambian history. A freedom fighter for the nation’s independence in the 1960s, he set up a national academy for science and trained a group of “afronauts” in the hope of beating the US and the Soviet Union in the race to reach the moon. Nkoloso, a kind of Dead Poets Society inspiration figure here, picks 17-year-old Martha (Ama Qamata) for the mission.

items.title: Why Gangtok Could Be India’s Most Walkable City!
items.blurb: #thebetterindia What if Indian cities were designed for people, not just cars? Gangtok, the capital of Sikkim, is showing us how! 🌿 While pedestrians across India struggle with encroached footpaths, traffic congestion and unsafe roads, Gangtok is setting an example in sustainable urban planning and pedestrian-friendly infrastructure. From protected footpaths, tactile tiles for visually impaired pedestrians and solar studs to underground utility ducts and elevated walkways, the city makes walking safer and more accessible. A 12-km footpath along its main highway connects neighbourhoods all the way to Ranipool, allowing people to walk without competing with vehicles for space. In 2009, Gangtok transformed its iconic MG Marg into a vehicle-free zone. No Horn Zones, ₹1,000 fines for unnecessary honking and odd-even traffic rules further help manage urban congestion. Gangtok offers a powerful lesson in sustainable mobility, accessible infrastructure and people-centric urban development. Walkable cities aren't just about convenience. They encourage healthier lifestyles, strengthen communities and reduce dependence on cars. Because a city shouldn't just make space for vehicles. It should make space for PEOPLE. items.title: No Forest Fires in 20+ Yrs: These Uttarakhand Women Revived 28 Acres of Barren Forest & Became Its Guardians
items.blurb: Every morning, 75-year-old Bhagirathi Devi walks into the forest beside her village in Uttarakhand's Champawat district. She patrols the area, returns home around noon and heads back for another round at 2 pm, often staying until sunset. Her task is to ensure that nobody cuts trees, damages vegetation or allows cattle to graze where they should not. For more than two decades, Bhagirathi has helped protect and restore this forest in Manar village. Known locally as Van Amma, she began the effort in 2000, when the woodland had become almost barren following years of excessive grazing and tree felling. Today, the community-managed forest is also a site of fire prevention. In a report published by Down To Earth on 31 May 2025, journalist Bhagirath documented how the village's women organised themselves to restore the forest, regulate access, and remove dry leaves and pine needles before the fire season. According to residents, there has been no forest fire in the restored forest since the initiative began. The Champawat Forest Department has also recognised the effort as a model for fire prevention. Manar's experience points to something important about forest protection in Uttarakhand: preventing fires is not always about reaching a burning hillside with firefighting equipment. It can begin much earlier, with people who understand the forest, depend on it and have the authority to regulate how it is used. Across the state's mountain villages, women are increasingly taking on this responsibility. As men migrate in search of employment, women remain to manage agriculture, livestock and household needs. Their daily work brings them into close contact with forests, making them among the first to notice smoke and respond to small fires. The Ghost Village question: who is left to protect the forest? Uttarakhand's migration story is often told through the image of the ghost village: a settlement where houses remain locked, agricultural fields lie fallow, and only a handful of residents remain. The scale of depopulation is reflected in government figures cited in the 2021 report Locked Houses, Fallow Lands: Climate Change and Migration in Uttarakhand, India , prepared by The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI) and the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research. According to the 2011 Census, 1,048 of Uttarakhand's 16,793 revenue villages were uninhabited. A subsequent survey by the state's Rural Development and Migration Commission in 2018 identified another 734 villages that had become uninhabited after 2011. The report notes that depopulation has affected all 13 districts, although the problem is more pronounced in the hill districts. However, not every village affected by migration is entirely deserted. In many settlements, men have moved to towns and cities for work while women, children and older residents remain. Women continue cultivating fields, looking after cattle, collecting forest produce and caring for family members. This changes who is available to respond when a forest fire breaks out. In Manar, Bhagirathi Devi's initiative began with a problem familiar to many women in mountain villages. Before the forest was restored, women had to walk seven to eight kilometres to a neighbouring forest, Siddhmandir, to collect fodder and firewood. Bhagirathi told Down To Earth that this journey took five to six hours every day. The loss of nearby forest cover had also affected the flow of local springs. Restoring the woodland was therefore not simply a conservation exercise. It was an attempt to make village life more sustainable. For women who remain, the responsibility is consequently twofold: maintaining households in villages with fewer working-age residents and protecting the natural resources that make those settlements habitable. Why women are often the first to notice a fire The reasons women become first responders are closely connected to the division of labour in rural households. Collecting firewood and fodder, taking cattle to graze, gathering leaves and working on agricultural land are routine responsibilities for many women in Uttarakhand. These activities keep them in and around forests for several hours a day. When a fire begins, they may notice the first signs of smoke before it becomes visible from the village or reaches the attention of forest officials. A 2023 paper by researchers Ripu Daman Singh, Surabhi Gumber, R C Sundriyal, Jeet Ram and Surendra P Singh, published in Tropical Ecology , provides important context for understanding this relationship. Titled Chir pine forest and pre-monsoon drought determine spatial and temporal patterns of forest fires in Uttarakhand Himalaya , the research analysed satellite-derived fire data from 2002 to 2020 across 24 forest divisions in the state. Collecting firewood and fodder, taking cattle to graze, gathering leaves and working on agricultural land are routine responsibilities for many women in Uttarakhand. Photograph: (TBI-File picture) The researchers recorded 80,440 fire detections over the 19 years. Their analysis found that warmer pre-monsoon temperatures, a greater proportion of chir pine forest and lower winter and pre-monsoon rainfall together explained 56% of the variation in fire incidence. They also noted that human activities associated with farming and the collection of fuel and fodder influence the likelihood of fires. The paper specifically recommends examining changes in population distribution and communities' dependence on forests as part of effective fire management. This is where women's everyday relationship with forests becomes relevant. They are not simply residents living near a fire-prone landscape. Their livelihoods are directly connected to the condition of that landscape. A fire can mean losing fodder for cattle, travelling farther to collect fuelwood, spending additional hours searching for forest produce and, in some cases, losing agricultural resources. The relationship between gender and firefighting is not simply a question of who is more willing to respond. It is also a question of who is expected to undertake the work when the forest that sustains the household is threatened. In a report published by Mongabay on 8 September 2026, journalist Swati Thapa documented this pattern in Uttarakhand villages. Researcher Kavya Pandey of the Centre for Wildlife Studies, Bengaluru, told Thapa that traditional gender roles and women's responsibility for household work and caregiving help explain why they are often the first to respond to fires. This offers a field-level account of a wider connection between women's labour and forest protection. How a community can stop a fire before it spreads Manar offers a particularly useful example of what happens when women move beyond responding to individual fires and take responsibility for managing an entire forest. When Bhagirathi Devi began the initiative in 2000, she brought other women together to form a van panchayat, a community forest-management council. She was unanimously elected its first sarpanch. The initial work involved clearing and fencing parts of the degraded forest. The women also worked with BAIF Development Research Foundation, a Pune-based organisation involved in silvopasture initiatives in the region. Silvopasture combines trees, grasses and livestock management . The idea was to restore vegetation while ensuring that the community could continue to access fodder and other forest resources. With BAIF's support and training, residents fenced the woodland using stones and thorny plants. They cleared invasive species such as lantana and planted native trees and fodder species, including banj oak ( Quercus leucotrichophora ), angu ( Fraxinus micrantha ) and utish ( Alnus nepalensis ). For two years, grazing was prohibited to allow the vegetation to recover. It took another five to six years for the trees to establish themselves. According to Manju Manral, the first president of Manar's Silvopasture Management Committee, 11.6 hectares of forest were eventually revived. The work was not entirely voluntary. Down To Earth reported that women involved in the restoration received Rs 120 per day from BAIF. They voluntarily contributed 10% of their wages towards maintaining the forest. Each household also contributed Rs 20 a month towards Bhagirathi's salary for guarding the woodland. A separate 2022 field study by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, BAIF and the Centre for Ecology Development and Research also found that the forest under Manar's van panchayat was healthier than the forest outside its management area. What the 2026 fire season reveals In an assessment published on 2 June 2026 on the Indian Institute of Remote Sensing's (IIRS) Sudoor Manthan science portal , researchers Athira V Mukundan, Madhusmita Murmu, Chandra Mohan Bhatt and Arijit Roy analysed forest-fire activity across the state between January and May 2026. Using NASA's MODIS active-fire data, they recorded: January: 200 active-fire detections. February: 113 detections. March: 178 detections. April: 207 detections. May: 433 detections. The May figure represented a 109% increase over April. It also accounted for approximately 38% of all detections recorded between January and May. Pauri Garhwal recorded the highest cumulative number of detections during the five-month period, at 207, followed by Chamoli with 190 and Tehri Garhwal with 130. District level of fire detections in May, 2026 Photograph: (FIRMS, NASA via Indian Institute of Remote Sensing) The researchers also used Sentinel-2 satellite imagery to map burned areas in Pauri Garhwal. Comparing images from April with those captured between 25 and 28 May, they identified approximately 838.66 sq km of burned area. Most of this was classified as low-severity burning, while 0.94 sq km fell into the highest severity category. These figures are satellite-based detections and mapped burn areas, not a count of independently verified individual fires. Nevertheless, they show how quickly fire activity intensified towards the end of the pre-monsoon season. The 2023 research by Singh and his colleagues helps explain this seasonal pattern. Most fires in Uttarakhand occur between March and May, when temperatures rise, vegetation dries and fresh pine litter accumulates on the forest floor. The human cost of these fires can be severe. On 13 June 2024, four forest department personnel died while fighting a blaze in Binsar Wildlife Sanctuary in Almora district. According to a report by The Times of India on 14 June 2024, four others were seriously injured after the firefighting team was engulfed by flames. For women who fight smaller fires in community forests, the risks are no less real, particularly when they have no protective clothing, footwear or firefighting equipment. Besides, women's participation does not automatically translate into decision-making power. A 2026 research chapter by K Nagahama, published in Springer Proceedings in Earth and Environmental Sciences , examines women's participation in a Uttarakhand van panchayat through household surveys, interviews, forest surveys and long-term observations conducted between 2011 and 2023. The research examines an important distinction: being present in community forest management does not necessarily mean having equal authority over decisions or control over resources. The problem is also visible in the reporting from Uttarakhand. The Forest Fire Prevention and Management Scheme and India's National Action Plan on Forest Fires recognise the importance of early detection, community participation and coordinated firefighting. Photograph: (TBI-File Picture) In her September 2026 Mongabay investigation, Swati Thapa spoke to Laxmi Kharayat, a field trainer with The Hunger Project, who described cases where women formally listed as van panchayat heads were unaware of their positions, while male family members exercised authority on their behalf. There is also a gap between the work women undertake and the employment opportunities available to them. Seasonal fire watchers recruited by the forest department are predominantly men. Women who assist in firefighting often do so without regular wages or access to appropriate protective equipment. The Forest Fire Prevention and Management Scheme and India's National Action Plan on Forest Fires recognise the importance of early detection, community participation and coordinated firefighting. The challenge is to ensure that these provisions translate into practical support for women at the village level. This means providing women with training in fire prevention and safe firefighting, protective clothing, gloves, sturdy footwear, communication equipment and access to emergency assistance. It also means creating paid opportunities for women as seasonal fire watchers and ensuring that they have actual decision-making authority within van panchayats. Just as importantly, their work should not be treated as an unpaid extension of household responsibilities simply because they are the people who remain in the village. Forest protection begins with the people who depend on it Bhagirathi Devi's work did not begin with a firefighting operation. It began with a forest that had become too degraded to support the people living beside it. By bringing women together, restoring native vegetation, regulating grazing and establishing a system for removing dry litter, the village created a model of long-term community protection. For women in Uttarakhand's mountain villages, protecting a forest also means protecting the resources that keep their households functioning. When the forest burns, the consequences reach their cattle, farms, water sources and daily routines. Their leadership has shown that communities can play a significant role in preventing fires, provided they have the authority and resources to do so. The next step is to ensure that this responsibility does not remain invisible or unpaid. The women who recognise the first signs of smoke, organise their neighbours and maintain village forests should be treated as essential partners in forest protection, not as an informal firefighting force expected to manage with whatever tools they have at hand. Sources: ‘Guardians of groves-How women of an Uttarakhand village successfully revived a lost forest’ : By Bhagirath, Published on 31 May 2025 ‘How Uttarakhand’s women and villages are defending forests with community, care and smart tools’ : By Varsha Singh, Published on 16 June 2025 ‘Forest commons for multiple benefits: Restoration of degraded land and revival of springs in Uttarakhand, India’ : By Dinesh Prasad Raturi, Santosh Paudel & Erica Udas, Published on 14 October 2022 ‘Chir pine forest and pre-monsoon drought determine spatial, and temporal patterns of forest fires in Uttarakhand Himalaya’ : By Ripu Daman Singh, Surabhi Gumber, R. items.title: What happened when the man who took a million photographs embraced colour?
items.blurb:
The Photographers’ Gallery, London
Sanlé Sory is known for his black and white images taken during independence in Burkina Faso – but his colour portraits bring humour, insouciance and joy

Despite his wide renown, there have been hardly any major exhibitions of Sanlé Sory’s work. His last UK show was in 2019, concentrating on the black-and-white images the Burkinabé photographer made in the first two decades after opening his own studio, Volta Photo, in Bobo-Dioulasso in 1960 – a period that coincided with the first two decades of independence in Burkina Faso. This new Photographer’s Gallery show shifts the focus to the 1980s and 1990s, when Sory began working in colour.

It’s easy to see why, even with few exhibitions, Sory has made such an impression on audiences. There are the familiar west African studio photography tropes westerners love, where sound, image, fashion and pose collide. The props are popping, the style is irrepressible, the energy is irresistible. I wonder if Sory’s speed and instinct came from the time he spent early in his career racing on his motorbike to photograph car accidents for newspapers and the police. These portraits are the opposite of a car crash, they’re remedially joyful, wilfully alive – but they share that feeling of being inside the moment, at the edge of something.

items.title: Meet the Young Innovator Using Data to Understand India’s Vanishing Groundwater
items.blurb: A borewell can run dry without much warning. For a farmer depending on it to irrigate crops or a family relying on it for everyday water needs, the question that follows is simple: how much water is actually left underground? Finding an answer is not easy. Unlike rivers, lakes, or reservoirs, groundwater reserves cannot be seen. Their availability depends on several factors, from rainfall and soil conditions to the rate at which water is extracted. Without reliable estimates, planning how much to draw or where to focus conservation efforts becomes difficult. By analysing historical borewell records, rainfall patterns and soil characteristics, JALAAKAR attempts to make underground water reserves easier to understand. Photograph: ( Firstpost ) A school student from Surat, Gujarat, is exploring how technology could make this information easier to access. Dheyay Shah has developed JALAAKAR, a machine-learning-based tool that estimates groundwater availability across different talukas using historical records and environmental data. His innovation recently won the national title at vivo Ignite 2026, a nationwide challenge that received more than 6,100 project submissions from school students across India. Making groundwater easier to understand India depends heavily on groundwater for drinking water, agriculture and other everyday needs. However, excessive extraction, changing rainfall patterns and growing demand have put pressure on these underground reserves. One of the difficulties in managing this resource is knowing how much water is available in a particular area. Groundwater levels can vary depending on local geography, the amount of rainfall received, and how much water is being extracted. This is where Dheyay's project comes in. Instead of relying on isolated measurements, JALAAKAR brings together different sources of information to generate estimates that help people better understand groundwater conditions. How JALAAKAR uses machine learning At its core, JALAAKAR uses machine learning to identify patterns in historical groundwater and environmental data. The tool considers information such as past borewell records, rainfall patterns, and soil characteristics. Each of these offers a different piece of information about underground water reserves. For instance, rainfall influences how much water can seep into the ground and replenish aquifers. Soil characteristics determine how readily this water can percolate, while borewell records provide insights into changes in groundwater levels over time. JALAAKAR analyses these datasets to identify relationships and recurring patterns. It then uses what it learns from the historical information to estimate groundwater availability at the taluka level. JALAAKAR uses historical data to identify patterns and estimate groundwater availability across different talukas. Photograph: ( Digit ) In simpler terms, the tool attempts to use what has happened in the past to understand what groundwater conditions might look like in a particular area. Such estimates could eventually help local communities, farmers, and those involved in water management make more informed decisions about extraction and conservation. However, predictive estimates are not a substitute for actual groundwater measurements. The tool's accuracy, independent field validation, and suitability for different geographical conditions would need to be established before it can be used for wider water-management decisions. A young innovator looking beneath the surface Dheyay's project was recognised at vivo Ignite 2026, where he emerged as the national winner. The competition brought together school students working on ideas that apply science and technology to real-world challenges. With more than 6,100 projects received, the challenge evaluated innovations on parameters such as creativity, scientific application, feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and potential social impact. What makes JALAAKAR interesting is the problem it chooses to address. Groundwater management is often discussed in terms of large-scale infrastructure and policy, but it also begins with something much simpler: understanding how much water is available before using it. Dheyay's innovation won the national title at vivo Ignite 2026. Photograph: ( Tehelka ) Dheyay's work explores how data can help answer that question. While the tool would need further testing and refinement before wider application, it offers a promising starting point for making groundwater information more accessible. For a young student, looking beneath the surface has meant looking at a problem that affects millions of people. And if developed further, JALAAKAR could contribute to a future where communities have better information to guide how they use and protect one of their most important natural resources. Sources: 'Dheyay Shah named winner for Vivo Ignite 2026, over 6,100 projects received' by Economic Times, Published on 29 October 2026. 'Surat school student uses machine learning to estimate groundwater availability; project wins national innovation challenge' by Sanjay Sharma for The Times Of India, Published on 10 November 2026.

items.title: From Hiring Disabled People to Helping Artisans Earn: 5 CEOs Building a Better India
items.blurb: What comes to mind when you think of a successful business? Crores in revenue, thousands of employees, a presence across the world, or perhaps a celebrated CEO? Now consider a few other measures of success. How many women earned their first independent income? How many people with disabilities found a workplace where they could build a career? How many families could afford life-saving medical treatment? How many rural artisans could earn a living without leaving their villages? Recent conversations around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s management practices have brought a larger question into focus: what truly makes a good business leader? Closer to home, these five Indian enterprises offer a different perspective on success. From hospitality and healthcare to waste management and handicrafts, they show how building a profitable business can go hand in hand with creating meaningful opportunities and improving people's lives. Making room for every ability At Lemon Tree Hotels, learning Indian Sign Language is part of employee training. It helps colleagues communicate with one another and makes everyday working life more accessible for employees with hearing disabilities. At Lemon Tree Hotels, employees learn Indian Sign Language to build a workplace where everyone can communicate and thrive. Photograph: ( Hotelier India ) Patu Keswani, the founder of the hotel group, began hiring people with disabilities in 2007. Over the years, the company has adapted its training programmes to accommodate people with different needs. Deaf employees receive training with the help of sign language interpreters, while colleagues with low vision are provided accessible learning materials. Some neurodivergent employees undergo internships lasting more than six months to help them settle into their roles. According to its 2025–26 annual report , Lemon Tree employed 305 people with disabilities and another 635 people from socially and economically disadvantaged backgrounds across its owned, leased and managed hotels. Much like several inclusive cafés across India , the hotel chain demonstrates how adapting workplaces to people's needs can open up meaningful career opportunities. Taking village crafts to the world In 1978, Nand Kishore Chaudhary began Jaipur Rugs with two looms and nine artisans. He wanted to connect rural craftspeople directly with larger markets, helping them earn through skills they had developed over generations. Jaipur Rugs connects 40,000 artisans across 600 villages to global markets, creating livelihoods through generations-old weaving skills. Photograph: ( Forbes India ) According to the founder's website , the business has grown to work with around 40,000 artisans across 600 villages in five Indian states. Around 80 percent of them are women. For many of these women, weaving offers an opportunity to earn from their homes without having to migrate to cities or travel far for work. As The Better India previously reported , the company delivers raw materials to artisans' homes and collects the finished carpets from them. Through its Manchaha initiative, artisans also get the freedom to create their own rug designs, drawing inspiration from their surroundings, experiences and imagination. Their craftsmanship has found customers across the world while creating livelihood opportunities closer to home. Making life-saving surgeries affordable For a family struggling to afford heart surgery, the cost of treatment can stand between a loved one and potentially life-saving medical care. It was this challenge that cardiac surgeon Dr Devi Shetty sought to address when he founded Narayana Health in Bengaluru in 2001. Narayana Health's high-volume hospital model helps reduce treatment costs, making specialised cardiac care accessible to more families. Photograph: ( GovInsider ) His hospital model focuses on performing a large number of surgeries, making efficient use of medical equipment and reducing procurement and operational expenses. The savings help bring down the cost of treatment for patients. A 2017 case study by The Commonwealth Fund documented that Narayana Health had brought the average cost of open-heart surgery below US$2,000 at the time. By rethinking how hospitals operate, Dr Shetty built a business model that demonstrates how greater efficiency can help more families access specialised medical care. Helping waste pickers become entrepreneurs When Lotfar moved to Bengaluru in 2010, he was struggling to make ends meet as a waste picker. A 2022 report by Tata Trusts documented how his life changed after he began working with Hasiru Dala. By then, he owned four trucks and employed around 20 other waste pickers. Founded in 2015 by Shekar Prabhakar, Nalini Shekar and Marwan Abubaker, Hasiru Dala Innovations is a waste management enterprise that helps informal waste workers build more secure livelihoods and run their own businesses. Hasiru Dala Innovations helps waste pickers become entrepreneurs, creating businesses around the people who keep cities clean. Photograph: ( Forbes India ) These entrepreneurs provide waste collection and management services to residential communities, offices and events. They earn through service fees as well as the sale of recyclable materials. By 2022, the enterprise had supported 24 waste-picker entrepreneurs, who had, in turn, created employment opportunities for around 300 other waste pickers. The model brings the people who have long helped keep our cities clean into the business of managing their waste, giving them opportunities to grow as entrepreneurs. From making papads to becoming business owners In 1959, seven women in Mumbai borrowed Rs 80 and began making papads. Their aim was simple: to earn an income of their own. What began as a small venture became Shri Mahila Griha Udyog Lijjat Papad, one of India's most recognisable household brands. Lijjat Papad provides self-employment to around 45,000 women, giving them a shared stake in the enterprise. Photograph: (Femina) According to its official website , the enterprise provides self-employment to around 45,000 women across 83 branches in 16 states. What makes Lijjat particularly interesting is its shared ownership model. Its women members participate in running the enterprise, and the profits and losses of each branch are shared among its members. For thousands of women, a skill they already possessed became a means of earning an income and having a stake in the business they helped build. More than six decades later, the enterprise offers an example of what women can achieve when they have access to economic opportunities and collective ownership. These five enterprises have taken different paths to growth. Yet, each offers a valuable lesson in how businesses can widen access to opportunities, recognise overlooked talent and help people build better lives for themselves. Perhaps, alongside asking how much a business earns, we could also ask a question that deserves just as much attention: Who grows when the business grows? items.title: India Records a 38% Drop in TB Deaths: What Are Key Public Health Efforts Behind the Progress?
items.blurb: A tuberculosis diagnosis can change a person’s life. Finding the disease early, starting the right treatment and helping a patient complete it can change that course again. India’s latest figures suggest these interventions are making a measurable difference. The World Health Organization’s (WHO) Global Tuberculosis Report 2026 estimates that India’s TB mortality rate fell from 28 deaths per lakh people in 2015 to 18 in 2025, a reduction of 38%. This is higher than the global decline of 35%. The figure reflects a public health response combining active screening, faster diagnosis, treatment and support beyond the clinic. The opportunity now is to extend these solutions and make care easier to access and complete. Finding TB before it finds the patient TB detection has often depended on people recognising symptoms and reaching a health facility. But symptoms can be overlooked or hidden by stigma. Active case-finding changes the approach: health teams take screening into communities and prioritise people at higher risk. Behind every percentage point of progress are lives saved through earlier diagnosis and sustained care. Photograph: ( Deccan Herald ) The TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, launched in November 2024, has expanded community-based screening. The Union Health Ministry says more than 25 crore people had been screened by November 2026, including over 11 crore chest X-rays and three crore molecular tests. The campaign reported detecting nearly 48.64 lakh cases, including almost 15 lakh people without symptoms. These are programme figures, not estimates of everyone with TB in India. Chest X-rays help identify people who need further testing, including those without obvious symptoms. Molecular tests can confirm TB and, depending on the test, identify drug resistance. WHO also records a rise in rapid testing: these tests were used for 46% of notified cases in 2025, up from 38% in 2024. Earlier diagnosis can mean earlier treatment, fewer opportunities for transmission and a better chance of preventing severe illness. It can also connect patients to appropriate treatment sooner, particularly when drug resistance is involved. Treatment needs support beyond medicine TB treatment usually lasts several months. Staying on medication can be difficult for people managing lost wages, food insecurity, travel costs, or stigma. A patient-centred response must address these barriers alongside the infection. The Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana provides nutritional support during TB treatment. Individuals and organisations can also register as Ni-kshay Mitras to offer patients additional assistance. These measures recognise that nutrition and practical support can influence a person’s ability to continue treatment and recover. From door-to-door screening to rapid testing, India is taking the fight against TB closer to communities. Photograph: ( The Indian Express ) The government reported a 94% treatment success rate among people treated for drug-susceptible TB. This does not describe outcomes for every person with TB, including those with drug-resistant disease. For people facing long journeys or uncertain incomes, local follow-up can make the difference between starting and completing treatment. Linking health workers, families and community organisations helps keep patients connected to care. Counselling and follow-up can help patients navigate treatment. A TB patient support initiative illustrates why guidance matters alongside medicines. Accounts of people who have recovered from drug-resistant TB underline the importance of timely testing, appropriate treatment and sustained support. Turning progress into wider access The 38% decline measures a reduction in estimated deaths, not a fall in infections by the same proportion. Incidence counts new and recurrent cases arising in a population over time; mortality estimates deaths caused by the disease. WHO has not published a new incidence estimate for India in its 2026 report. The estimates are under review while district-level surveillance data collected in 2025 are analysed. Updated figures are expected in early 2027. The previous report estimated a 21% decline in incidence between 2015 and 2024, from 237 to 187 cases per lakh. This remains the latest comparable estimate, not a 2025 figure. The data gap makes stronger surveillance and reliable local information important. So is taking screening and diagnosis to remote and underserved communities. Rural health screening initiatives offer one way to bring early detection closer to people. TB specialists have also highlighted why treatment must be accompanied by attention to nutrition, living conditions and other health risks. India’s progress has come from combining different parts of the response: finding people earlier, improving access to rapid tests, supporting patients during treatment and strengthening community participation. The next step is to make these services dependable wherever a person lives, with prompt drug-resistance testing, uninterrupted medicines, nutritional support and follow-up. A fall in deaths means more people are surviving. Sustaining that progress will depend on ensuring fewer people are missed, and everyone diagnosed with TB can access and complete effective treatment. The 38% decline is a reason to build on what is working. items.title: What Happens to Your Old Clothes? Inside a Mumbai Network Turning 17500 Kg Into Income for Traders & Artisans
items.blurb: “Bhandiwala, bhandiwala.” For years, the familiar call was part of how 35-year-old Anil Datanini earned a living. Like other bhandiwalas , he collected old clothes , traditionally exchanged for utensils, and sold what could be reused. He had entered the trade at around 15, following work his family knew well. After moving from Gujarat to Mumbai, he continued sorting textiles and finding buyers for them. But there was one thing he could never count on: how much material he would find. Some days brought plenty of clothes; on others, hours spent looking for them yielded very little. That began to change in January 2026, when Anil partnered with Textile Waste Innovation Network (TWIN), a Mumbai-based enterprise founded by 29-year-old Vikram Shahi. Instead of sourcing everything himself, Anil now receives a more regular supply of used clothes, which he sorts, prepares and sells through markets in villages and rural areas. “Now the material comes to us regularly, so we can work properly,” he says. “We sort it according to the quality and condition and then send the reusable clothes to villages.” Anil says he currently earns between Rs 25,000 and Rs 30,000 a month, sometimes more. For him, the greater relief is being able to plan household expenses and save with more confidence. His experience captures an important part of TWIN's approach. According to its founder, the network has collected around 17,500 kg of used textiles and reached more than 650 households. It is doing so by working with waghari workers and bhandiwalas , whose experience in collecting and reselling clothes has long kept usable fabric in circulation. From his mother's cupboard to Mumbai's beaches When Vikram was growing up in Mumbai, he watched his mother exchange old clothes for steel utensils with a bhandiwala . He understood the exchange, but wondered what happened to those clothes afterwards. Even where recycling or upcycling options existed, there was no obvious route connecting a household's unwanted textiles to the people who could process them. Born in Bihar, with family roots in Sitamarhi, Vikram moved to Mumbai with his parents when he was three. In 2017, while studying information technology at Mumbai University, he began volunteering at clean-up drives. At Versova beach that monsoon, he noticed clothes mixed in with the plastic waste. He saw more discarded textiles during subsequent clean-ups, including around festivals such as Holi. In 2019, he began organising drives of his own with support from Bhumi NGO. The question from his childhood returned: where did damaged clothes go when they were no longer useful to their owners? In 2022, Vikram enrolled for a master's in social work at the College of Social Work, Nirmala Niketan, Mumbai. A term paper on waste management helped him explore what happens to post-consumer textiles, meaning clothes and other fabrics discarded after use. “Post-consumer textile waste was not getting the kind of attention I felt it deserved,” he tells The Better India . The gap became clearer in 2024, when he joined ReCircle as a sales executive. He had initially applied to work in plastic waste management, but was offered a role involving textiles instead. “At that point, I did not know much about textile waste, but once I started working on it, I realised there was a huge gap in the collection system,” he says. People had familiar ways of passing on clothes that were still wearable: donating them, giving them to relatives or exchanging them for utensils. Torn T-shirts, worn-out bedsheets and other unusable fabric were more difficult to deal with. Even where recycling or upcycling options existed, there was no obvious route connecting a household's unwanted textiles to the people who could process them. A 1,200-kg experiment in the Mumbai monsoon In August 2025, while working full time on education initiatives, including STEM labs in schools, Vikram and a few friends organised a textile collection drive in Vasai. They gathered around 1,200 kg of material, despite heavy monsoon rain complicating the collection. Vikram continued his job until February 2026, when he began focusing on the enterprise full time. “I was still working at the time, so we were doing this mostly on weekends,” he recalls. “The first drive itself gave us confidence that people actually had this problem and were looking for a solution.” TWIN was formally registered on 30 October 2025. Vikram continued his job until February 2026, when he began focusing on the enterprise full time. He wanted to make textile collection easier for households while giving existing recovery workers a more dependable source of material. “We are not trying to replace the existing recovery network. We are trying to build on it and create a more organised collection layer around it,” he explains. What happens to clothes after TWIN collects them? TWIN collects used textiles from households, housing societies, schools, colleges, hotels, companies, NGOs and other bulk generators across the Mumbai Metropolitan Region. Household pickups are described by the enterprise as free. A resident can request a collection through TWIN's website or WhatsApp chatbot, sharing their name, location and details of the textiles. The team records the request, including the quantity and type of material, in a customer relationship management system (CRM) before verifying it and assigning a collection partner. The enterprise works with waghari and bhandiwala workers, providing training, checking backgrounds and assigning collection areas by PIN code. This helps coordinate pickups that were previously handled more informally. The collected clothes are then sorted by condition, fabric and possible next use. That step determines whether a shirt can be worn again or whether a damaged bedsheet might be more useful as raw material for another product. He wanted to make textile collection easier for households while giving existing recovery workers a more dependable source of material. “Sorting is one of the most important parts because every textile cannot go to the same place,” Vikram says. “We look at the condition, quality and what the next best use can be.” Wearable clothes are prioritised for reuse. Workers sell them through their existing networks in villages and second-hand markets, where buyers, including farmers, can find affordable clothing. A smaller share goes to communities through NGO partners. Fabric unsuitable for wearing can take a different route. TWIN sends suitable material to upcycling partners, including The Kapda Project and artisan groups, to be made into bags, pouches and bottle holders. It also helps connect these products with buyers, including through organisations such as Sparkling Wings and Prayas Foundation. Lower-grade textiles may be downcycled into mats, rags or wiping cloths for industrial use. Recycling remains at the pilot stage, with TWIN and its partners testing which materials can be processed further. The network therefore offers several recovery routes, rather than claiming that every collected item becomes a new garment or recycled fibre. For residents, the idea is straightforward: clothes that have outlived their original use need different destinations. TWIN says it accepts wearable and torn clothes, bedsheets and curtains, but not wet or soiled material. That distinction matters when someone is clearing out a cupboard and wondering what can actually be collected. ‘Now we get clothes regularly, so there is more work’ TWIN currently works with around 15 to 20 informal textile recovery workers, of whom seven to 10 are connected to a more regular supply. Some receive around 200 to 300 kg of sorted textiles from the warehouse in a week, while others collect material directly from households. TWIN currently works with around 15 to 20 informal textile recovery workers, of whom seven to 10 are connected to a more regular supply. Anil, who has lived in the Sion-Dharavi area, says this has changed how he organises his work. Earlier, much of his time went into finding textiles before he could begin sorting and selling them. Now he can spend more of it preparing clothes for buyers. “We had to go and search for clothes ourselves,” he says. “Sometimes we would get material and sometimes we would not. The supply was not regular.” For 22-year-old Bhavesh Dattani, the difference feels familiar. He grew up in Dharavi, where his family continued a clothes-trading livelihood after his grandparents moved from Gujarat. Before joining TWIN in December 2025, he went from neighbourhood to neighbourhood exchanging utensils for clothes. “The barter system takes a lot of time. We have to go from place to place and ask people for clothes, and we do not know how much we will collect,” he says. Now, he receives reusable garments from the team. “Now we get clothes regularly, so there is more work and the income is also more regular,” he adds. He does not specify his earnings, but says having material available more consistently has improved his working routine. Another worker, Vikram Shankar Chekhaliya, about 45, comes from a family in Gujarat that has worked with textiles for generations. Associated with the initiative since its early stages in July 2025, he had previously sourced, sorted and sold clothes independently, including lower-value fabric used for wiping. “Sometimes we would get good clothes, and sometimes there would be very little material. Now there is a regular supply, so it becomes easier to plan the work,” he says. These workers already know how to assess clothing and where it can be sold. What TWIN is trying to add is a more predictable connection between the households discarding textiles and the markets that can use them. Who earns what when an old shirt is sold again? Although household pickups are free, the enterprise earns through the sale and recovery of collected material, as well as service-based work with organisations. Upcycled products made by partner artisans create another income stream when they are purchased by organisations or corporate clients. Reusable clothes move through existing traders and markets, allowing workers to earn from their sale. TWIN also generates revenue from recovered textiles. Upcycled products made by partner artisans create another income stream when they are purchased by organisations or corporate clients. Lower-grade materials can be sold for uses such as industrial wiping, while business-to-business services add to the model. “The idea is not just to collect waste and then store it,” Vikram says. “There has to be a value chain after collection. We need to make sure the material moves to the right person or the right organisation and that there is a revenue stream to sustain the system.” Vikram began with his own resources. TWIN has also received support from Mumbai Ekatra, a citizen-focused grant programme, particularly for its upcycling work. According to Vikram, the enterprise has generated about Rs 3 lakh in business revenue, with another Rs 3 lakh worth of potential business in the pipeline. It has yet to turn profitable, he says, with much of its income being put back into building the collection and sorting network. 17,500 kg of clothes collected. What comes next? The WhatsApp chatbot, launched in June 2026 after TWIN initially relied on Instagram and a Google Form, has made it easier to organise incoming requests. Vikram says it recorded more than 300 registrations in its first month. The team can also track where clothes are coming from, how much is collected and which partner should handle each pickup. Technology helps manage the movement of textiles, but the recovery itself still depends on people who know how to sort, repair, reuse or sell them. For now, the work is focused on Mumbai. Vikram hopes to expand to other cities, adapting the collection network to the workers, markets and waste patterns already present in each place. There are challenges ahead. Recycling is still being tested , the enterprise is not profitable and only part of its worker network currently receives a regular supply. The team can track where clothes are coming from, how much is collected and which partner should handle each pickup. But the model has begun to connect two needs that often sit apart: households looking for a responsible way to part with old textiles, and workers looking for material they can earn from. For Anil, that connection has a practical meaning. He still sorts clothes, finds buyers and does the work he has known since his teens. What has changed is the amount of time he needs to spend searching for the next batch, and the confidence that there will be work to return to. All pictures courtesy Vikram Shahi.

items.title: The Guardian view on disability benefits: Timms’s radical review is rooted in experience | Editorial
items.blurb:
Ministers have taken on board their MPs’ message about cuts. Now anxious claimants need reassurance

Four million people with disabilities or long‑term health conditions in the UK claim personal independence payment (Pip). A review by Sir Stephen Timms, the social security minister, offers a blueprint for how to overhaul it. Its recommendations pose a difficult question for ministers: are they prepared to meet the needs that a more accurate assessment of the costs of disability might reveal?

Sir Stephen worked as one of three co-chairs with a steering group of 12 people with a range of professional and lived experience. There is broad agreement that Pip needs to be reformed. The announcement on Tuesday that the government would accept the recommendation of a new fast track for claimants whose conditions are lifelong or unlikely to improve, and abolish unnecessary benefit reviews, signalled that ministers are ready for change. The decision, affecting one in 10 claimants in England and Wales, is welcome but long overdue. Ministers should work with the devolved administrations to ensure similar progress elsewhere in the UK.

items.title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham and Wales: a devolution blindspot at No 10 | Editorial
items.blurb:
The PM has summarily dismissed Welsh demands for further powers similar to those enjoyed in Scotland. The approach seems at odds with his consensual style

As he headed for Downing Street this summer, Andy Burnham said that he aimed to be “as collaborative and pragmatic as possible” in his dealings with the governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. His predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, had notoriously warned ministers against being “overly deferential” in discussions with the devolved administrations. But Mr Burnham’s signature commitment to distributing more power and responsibility out of Westminster, and his consensual style, appeared to augur well for a positive reset in relations.

In Wales, this early optimism has just been brutally quashed by an uncharacteristically peremptory letter from Mr Burnham to the first minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth. In it, the prime minister flatly rejected Welsh calls for the devolving of powers in relation to policing and justice, the crown estate and rail infrastructure. In the case of policing, Mr Burnham is in the curious position of denying to Mr ap Iorwerth the type of power that he enjoyed as the mayor of Greater Manchester.

items.title: Farage preaches the Brexit gospel according to St Nige | John Crace
items.blurb:
Reform leader is happy to return to his anti-EU happy place, where the truth can be whatever you want it to be

This feels like Nigel Farage’s happy place. It’s hardly a secret that he prefers his own company. His fellow Reform MPs are a necessary inconvenience at best. Muppets at worst. He can barely hide his misogyny for Sarah Pochin, having written her off as a pisshead. Nor does he have a much higher opinion of Richard Tice, Zia Yusuf and the others. But even Nige has worked out that when it comes to having a Potemkin alternative cabinet, he can’t realistically do everything himself.

Only when it comes to Brexit, it seems, is Farage at his best as a one-man band. This is his battle. During Monday’s Commons statement, Andy Burnham said he didn’t want to keep “banging on about Europe”. But Nige most definitely does. Not least because the more he can talk about Brexit, the less people will criticise him for having no real plans for government. Most of his domestic policies collapse on contact with reality. As for foreign policy, he doesn’t have one. Unless you count having as little to do with the EU as possible.

By chance, I found myself committed to a debate with people whose views I share. It was an eye-opening experience

I was on a panel recently in a church – St Luke’s in Battersea, south London – about the future of the welfare state, except the other panellists booked to speak on the right of politics were unwell and couldn’t come. And so we ended up with an entirely leftwing panel (albeit different shades of the left).

Puckishly, I suggested that I would split my six minutes of allocated speaking time and do three on what the rightwing panellists would have said, had they appeared, and then three on why they are wrong. But I couldn’t get the arguments right. I know they think the current welfare bill is – between our ageing population, our Neets and our dated expectations about what a decent life looks like and whose job it is to ensure you have one – “unsustainable”. I just couldn’t summon the right mix of tough-minded realism and benign resignation to other people’s misery. It wouldn’t come out of my mouth.

items.title: Council tax and stamp duty: both are a disaster zone. Scrap them and start from scratch | Polly Toynbee
items.blurb:
These ancient and often grossly unfair taxes are stifling the economy and young people. It’s long past time for radical reform

When voters were asked in 2020 which tax they would cut first, council tax came out on top, and rightly so. Still, it’s taken six years for an array of Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs to call for reforms to this most grotesquely unjust tax.

Prompted by a public petition organised by the campaign Fairer Share, a Westminster Hall debate heard calls for a review into property taxes, which would lay out options for replacing council tax and stamp duty land tax. Labour MPs were among those who have signed a letter to Downing Street calling for property tax reform to be a priority in Andy Burnham’s upcoming 10-year plan. Among flotillas of economists and thinktanks who signed the letter is Lord O’Neill, a Burnham adviser and former Goldman Sachs economist, who calls UK property taxation “utterly nonsensical”. Burnham has frequently backed reform of the “highly regressive” council tax and stamp duty, labelling them as “a tax on the aspiration of young people”.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

items.title: Millennial Democrats used social media in the midterms to sell their policies – and their personalities
items.blurb:
Through snappily produced videos and cultural riffing, candidates like Abdul El-Sayed, Annie Andrews and Scott Colom fully bought into the medium

Dancing in a cowboy hat. Trick-or-treating. Lampooning the typical conservative woman. Auditioning for a rip-off of Love Island.

The 2026 midterms were marked by Democrats’ sweeping success across the country, but also by a noticeable shift in how the candidates used social media. From Texas to Mississippi to Michigan, voters were treated to an array of parodies and takedowns, as millennial Democrats, in particular, used Instagram and TikTok to sell not just their policies, but their personalities.

items.title: ‘Is it possible for any government to run that way?’: Americans outraged over tech outages
items.blurb:
After the nationwide flight stoppage and Microsoft outage, many are directing their anger at the Trump administration

The US Federal Aviation Administration’s grounding of all US flights last week, alongside separate outages affecting Microsoft services, caused widespread disruption across the country.

While flights and Microsoft applications have since returned to normal, readers across the US have shared their frustrations with the Guardian. Many have directed their anger at the Trump administration, questioning its competence and calling for greater accountability and transparency about the systems millions of people rely on.
